questions.q: Page code runs for (const b of document.querySelectorAll(".remove")) b.addEventListener("click", …) once at start-up. Why does the Remove button of an item added later do nothing?
questions.explain: Listeners belong to elements, not to selectors. A delegated listener on the list covers buttons added later, because their clicks bubble up to it.
options: Buttons created with createElement cannot receive clicks
The loop only attached listeners to the buttons that existed when it ran; the new button never got one
querySelectorAll returns a live list, which skips new elements
The new button needs isTrusted set to true

questions.q: A listener is on <ul id="cart">. The user clicks the <span class="icon"> inside a Remove button inside an <li>. What are event.target and event.currentTarget?
questions.explain: target is where the event happened: the innermost element, the icon. currentTarget is the element whose listener is running: the list. That is why delegated code uses event.target.closest("button").

questions.q: Three listeners exist: (A) on document with { capture: true }, (B) on a button, (C) on document with no options. The button is clicked. In which order do they run?
questions.explain: The capture phase goes down from window first (A), then the target (B), then the bubble phase goes back up (C).

questions.q: A form wants to highlight whichever field has focus with a single listener on the <form>. Which event should it listen for?
questions.explain: focus and blur are among the few events that do not bubble. Their twins focusin and focusout do, so they work with delegation. (Focus also changes with the Tab key, not only with clicks.)
options: focusin, because focus does not bubble and focusin does
click, because focus always comes from a click
change, because it fires when a field is focused

questions.q: A widget calls event.stopPropagation() in its click listener. What is the most likely side effect?
questions.explain: Stopping propagation hides the event from every listener further along the path. Other code that relies on the event bubbling silently breaks. Deciding with event.target is almost always better.
options: The widget's own button stops working
The browser's default action is cancelled
Listeners on ancestors, such as a document-level "close the menu on outside click" or analytics, never hear those clicks
Nothing, because stopPropagation only affects the capture phase

questions.q: What is the difference between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
questions.explain: They control two independent things. A link click with stopPropagation() still navigates; a link click with preventDefault() still reaches the document's listeners.
options: They are two names for the same thing
preventDefault cancels the browser's own action (navigate, tick, submit) but the event keeps travelling; stopPropagation stops the travel but not the default action
preventDefault stops the travel; stopPropagation cancels the default action
preventDefault only works in the capture phase

questions.q: What does { passive: true } on a touchmove listener mean?
questions.explain: Scrolling normally has to wait to see whether a listener cancels it. A passive listener cannot, so scrolling stays smooth. preventDefault() inside it is ignored.
options: The listener runs after all other listeners
A promise that the listener will not call preventDefault(), so the browser can scroll without waiting for it
The listener does not receive an event object

questions.q: Why does a delegated cart listener use event.target.closest("[data-action]") instead of reading event.target.dataset.action directly?
questions.explain: event.target is the innermost element clicked. closest checks that element and then its ancestors, so it finds the button whether the click hit the button or something inside it.
options: dataset is not available on event targets
The click may land on a child of the button, such as an icon or a text span, which has no data-action; closest walks up to the button
event.target is always the list, not the button

questions.q: Which event suits each job: (1) live search results while the user types, (2) saving a quantity once the user has finished editing the box?
questions.explain: input fires on every edit, including paste and autofill. change fires when the user commits a value, for a text box when they leave it after editing.

questions.q: Why handle a form's submit event instead of the submit button's click?
questions.explain: A form can be submitted in several ways; all of them fire submit on the form. Call preventDefault() there, or the browser sends the form and reloads the page.
options: click events do not bubble from buttons
submit also fires when the user presses Enter in a field, and it is where the browser's own sending can be cancelled
Buttons inside forms cannot have listeners

questions.q: What is the difference between form.requestSubmit() and form.submit()?
questions.explain: If your submit listener does validation or sends with fetch, calling form.submit() bypasses all of it. Use requestSubmit().
options: requestSubmit() acts like a user submit (validation and a submit event); submit() skips both and sends the form immediately

questions.q: A form has <input type="checkbox" name="leaveAtGate">. What does Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)) contain for it?
questions.explain: FormData follows what a browser would send: unticked checkboxes are left out, ticked ones send their value, which defaults to "on". All values are strings. Convert on the way in: data.leaveAtGate === "on".
options: leaveAtGate: "on" when ticked, and no leaveAtGate key at all when not ticked
Nothing: checkboxes are not included in FormData

questions.q: The cart refuses quantities above 20 and disables the Place order button while an order is being sent. Which statement is right?
questions.explain: Browser checks are for the user's convenience. A user can edit the page, or skip it and send requests with curl. The server is the only place rules can be enforced.
options: The server can now trust the quantities it receives
The server no longer needs to check prices, because the page computed the total
The server must still validate quantities, recompute prices and refuse duplicate orders, because anyone can send requests without the page
Disabling the button makes duplicate orders impossible

questions.q: Why does this fail to remove the listener?
questions.explain: Listeners are matched by identity. Keep the function in a variable, use { once: true }, or pass a signal and call abort().
options: Each arrow expression creates a new function object, so the second one is not the listener that was added
Listeners can only be removed inside the listener itself

questions.q: A view adds listeners to window, document and three buttons. What is the simplest reliable way to remove them all when the view closes?
questions.explain: An aborted signal removes every listener registered with it. The same signal can also cancel the view's pending fetch calls.
options: Call removeEventListener five times with new arrow functions
Pass one AbortController's signal to every addEventListener, then call controller.abort()

questions.q: A test calls button.click(). What is event.isTrusted in the listener, and why?
questions.explain: Only events generated by the browser from real user input are trusted. Browsers allow some actions (pop-ups, full screen, clipboard) only from trusted events. Never use isTrusted as a security check on the server's behalf.
options: true, because the button is a real element
false, because the event was created by code, not by the user
true only if the test runs in a real browser

questions.q: The cart runs widget.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:change", { detail })) and the header listens on document. The badge never updates. Why?
questions.explain: Built-in events like click bubble, but events you create default to bubbles: false, so only listeners on widget itself hear it.
options: Custom event names cannot contain a colon
Events created with new CustomEvent do not bubble unless you pass bubbles: true
Custom events are dispatched asynchronously, after the page has been drawn

questions.q: Which pairing is right?
questions.explain: A debounce waits for a quiet moment, so a search runs once per pause. A throttle runs at most once per period while events keep coming, so an indicator keeps moving without running on every event.
options: Search box: throttle. Scroll-position indicator: debounce
Search box: debounce (act once the user pauses). Scroll-position indicator: throttle (update regularly while scrolling)
Neither needs either; browsers limit events automatically

questions.q: Two scripts on a page both do checkoutButton.onclick = …. What happens?
questions.explain: An event-handler property is a single slot. addEventListener keeps a list, so independent scripts can each add their own listener.
options: Only the second handler runs: the property holds one function, and the second assignment replaced the first
The browser throws an error for the second assignment

questions.q: On a slow connection, a customer clicks Place order twice. Which change in the page prevents a second order from being sent?
questions.explain: The second submit arrives while the first is still waiting for the server. A flag checked at the start of the listener ignores it; disabling the button tells the user. The server should still refuse duplicates.
options: A submitting flag that makes the listener ignore submits while an order is in flight, plus disabling the button

questions.q: In the task list, a click on a task's title text (inside the <label> that wraps the checkbox) ticked the task. Why?
questions.explain: Labels forward clicks to their control. Listening for change on checkboxes covers mouse, label and keyboard toggles alike.
options: The title had its own click listener
Clicking a label clicks its checkbox (a default action), which toggles it and fires change, which the delegated listener handles
The browser ticks every checkbox in a list item that is clicked

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Listeners run in the order they were added. The once listener is removed after its first call, so the second dispatch only reaches badge.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Adding the same function twice (with the same options) registers it once, so the customer is charged once. The removal fails because it passes a different arrow function, so the logger stays.

questions.q: Is dispatchEvent synchronous? What does this print?
questions.explain: dispatchEvent calls every listener before it returns, like a normal function call. The microtask waits until the current code has finished.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: preventDefault() does nothing on an event that is not cancelable. For a cancelable one, dispatchEvent returns false to tell the code that dispatched it "a listener said no".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: stopImmediatePropagation also skips the remaining listeners on the same target. Plain stopPropagation would still have run send.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Aborting removed the two listeners that used the signal. A listener added later with an already aborted signal is never added at all, so scroll C never runs. Create a new controller for each new view.
options:
resize A
resize B
scroll A
end

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Events you create do not bubble unless you ask, and are never trusted. detail is whatever you passed. The kobo amount divided by 100 is 19300 naira; formatting with commas needs toLocaleString.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The three quick calls reset the same timer, so only the last one, "ric", runs, 50 ms later. The call at 200 ms starts a new burst of one, which runs too.
options:
search: r
search: ri
search: ric
search: rice
end

questions.q: This function models bubbling with parent links and a stop flag. What does it print?
questions.explain: Bubbling goes from the target upwards. The line's handler stops propagation, but the line itself still finishes (it is logged), and nothing above it is reached.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A passive listener promised not to cancel the event, so its preventDefault() is ignored (browsers print a warning in the developer console). The event counts as not cancelled.
options: TypeError: preventDefault is not allowed in a passive listener

questions.q: This models a delegated listener: find the nearest node with an action, then the nearest node above it with a sku. What does it print?
questions.explain: A click on the icon walks up to the button, like closest("[data-action]"). A click on the product name finds no action on its way up, so it is ignored, just as the cart ignored a click on a heading.
options:
remove garri-2kg
remove garri-2kg
remove garri-2kg

questions.q: Write debounce(fn, waitMs): it returns a function that, each time it is called, cancels the previous pending call and schedules fn with the latest arguments after waitMs. The program should print two searches.
questions.explain: The timer lives in the closure, so every call can cancel the one before. clearTimeout(undefined) is harmless, which keeps the first call simple.

questions.q: Write throttle(fn, periodMs, now). now() returns the current time in milliseconds (a test passes a fake clock). The first call runs; later calls run only if at least periodMs have passed since the last run.
questions.explain: Starting last at -Infinity lets the first call through. Injecting the clock makes timing code testable without waiting, the same idea as fake timers in Vitest.

questions.q: Make Cart extend EventTarget. add(sku, qty) adds to the quantity for that sku and dispatches a CustomEvent named "change" whose detail is { sku, qty, count }, where qty is the sku's new quantity and count the total number of items.
questions.explain: Extending EventTarget gives your object addEventListener and dispatchEvent in browsers and in Node.js. Remember to call super() if you write a constructor.

questions.q: Nodes are objects with an optional data object and a parent. Write closestWith(node, key) that returns the nearest node, starting at node, whose data has key, and handleClick(target) that returns "<action> <sku>" for a click inside an action button, or "ignored".
questions.explain: This is the shape of every delegated listener: find the control with closest, bail out if there is none, then find the item it belongs to. In the DOM, data is dataset and closestWith(n, "action") is n.closest("[data-action]").

questions.q: Write parseQuantity(text) for the cart's quantity box. Trim it; accept only whole numbers written with digits from 1 to 20 and return { qty }; otherwise return { error } with the message shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: A regular expression that allows only digits rejects signs, decimals, words and the empty string in one step. Number("") would be 0 and Number(" 3 ") 3, so testing the text first avoids surprises from JavaScript's conversions.

questions.q: Model what FormData collects. collect(fields) gets objects { name, type, value, checked } and returns an object: fields without a name are skipped, checkboxes are included only when checked (with their value, default "on"), and every value is a string.
questions.explain: These are the rules a real form follows. The unticked giftWrap is missing, not false, and the number arrives as the string "2": code that reads form data must convert and check every value.

questions.q: Write tryCheckout(cart). It dispatches a cancelable event "checkout:before" on cart and returns "placing order" if no listener cancelled it, otherwise "checkout cancelled". The listener below cancels when the cart is empty.
questions.explain: Without cancelable: true, preventDefault() would be ignored and every checkout would go ahead. dispatchEvent's return value is how the code that fired the event learns a listener said no.

questions.q: Write listenAll(target, types, handler) that adds handler for every event type in types and returns a stop() function that removes them all at once, using one AbortController.
questions.explain: One signal shared by every listener means one call removes them all. This is the clean-up pattern for a view or component that must not keep listening after it is gone.
